Securing Commerce Through Strength: The Case for Military Protection Clauses in International Trade Agreements

Introduction

Throughout history, the prosperity of great nations has depended not merely on the ingenuity of their merchants and entrepreneurs but on the willingness of their governments to safeguard commercial interests abroad. From the British Empire's deployment of naval forces to protect the East India Company to America's own Open Door Policy in China, the intertwining of military capability and commercial security has been a recurring feature of international relations. Today, as American corporations invest trillions of dollars across the globe — building infrastructure, creating jobs, and driving economic development in signatory nations — the question of how to protect those investments from expropriation, political instability, and lawless seizure has never been more urgent.

This essay argues that the United States should pursue the inclusion of explicit military intervention provisions in future international trade agreements — provisions that would authorize the deployment of American armed forces in signatory countries under defined circumstances to protect American corporate interests and investments. While such a proposal will inevitably face criticism from those who invoke sovereignty concerns and anti-interventionist sentiment, a careful examination reveals that such provisions would serve the interests of stability, the rule of law, economic development, and the international order itself.

I. The Scale and Vulnerability of American Investment Abroad

American foreign direct investment (FDI) abroad exceeded $6.5 trillion as of recent estimates. American corporations operate mines in sub-Saharan Africa, petroleum extraction facilities in the Middle East and South America, manufacturing plants across Southeast Asia, and technology infrastructure on every continent. These investments are not mere abstractions on a corporate balance sheet; they represent the retirement savings of millions of American workers whose pension funds are invested in multinational corporations, the livelihoods of American employees stationed abroad, and the tax revenues that fund essential domestic programs.

Yet these investments exist in an environment of considerable risk. Nationalization, expropriation without adequate compensation, civil unrest targeting foreign-owned facilities, and the selective application of domestic law to disadvantage American firms are well-documented phenomena. Venezuela's seizure of billions of dollars in American oil assets under Hugo Chávez, Bolivia's nationalization of natural gas facilities, and the repeated targeting of American agricultural investments in Zimbabwe all illustrate the vulnerability of American capital abroad. Existing mechanisms of recourse — investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) panels, International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) arbitration, and diplomatic negotiation — are slow, frequently unenforceable, and dependent on the cooperation of the very governments that initiated the expropriation.

The gap between the magnitude of American investment and the inadequacy of existing protections creates a compelling case for stronger measures. When billions of dollars and thousands of American jobs are at stake, paper arbitration mechanisms with no enforcement teeth are insufficient.

II. The Historical Precedent for Military-Commercial Linkage

The proposal to link military capability to trade protection is not a radical innovation; it is a return to principles that undergirded the most successful periods of global commerce. The Pax Britannica of the nineteenth century — widely regarded as one of the most prosperous eras in human history — was sustained in large part by Britain's willingness to use the Royal Navy to enforce commercial agreements, protect British subjects and investments abroad, and ensure freedom of navigation. The result was not merely British prosperity but a dramatic expansion of global trade that benefited nations at every level of development.

The United States itself has a long tradition of military-commercial protection. The Marine Corps' interventions in the Caribbean and Central America during the early twentieth century — whatever one thinks of their execution — were undertaken in part to protect American investments and ensure the stability of governments that had entered into commercial relationships with the United States. The deployment of naval forces to protect oil shipping lanes in the Persian Gulf during the Tanker War of the 1980s was an explicit use of military power to safeguard commercial interests. More recently, American military presence in the Middle East has been understood, in part, as a guarantor of energy market stability — a function that benefits not only the United States but the entire global economy.

These precedents demonstrate an important principle: the credible threat of military enforcement is often the most effective guarantor of commercial agreements. Nations that know their commitments will be enforced are far less likely to violate them.

III. Deterrence and Stability: The Primary Function of Intervention Provisions

Critics will likely characterize military intervention provisions as a recipe for perpetual warfare. In reality, the opposite is true. The primary function of such provisions would be deterrent, not operational. The explicit inclusion of military enforcement mechanisms in trade agreements would dramatically reduce the likelihood that signatory governments would engage in expropriation, contract abrogation, or targeted legal harassment of American firms.

This logic mirrors the well-established strategic principle of deterrence that has governed nuclear policy for decades. The United States does not maintain its nuclear arsenal with the expectation of use; it maintains it to ensure that adversaries understand the consequences of aggression, thereby preventing aggression from occurring. Similarly, an explicitly stated right of military intervention to protect American corporate interests would function primarily as a stabilizing mechanism. Governments contemplating the seizure of American assets would weigh the costs far more carefully if the possibility of military response were codified in an international agreement they had voluntarily signed.

The deterrent effect would also benefit domestic governance in signatory nations. Governments that are tempted to expropriate foreign assets often do so to shore up short-term domestic political support at the expense of long-term economic development. A credible deterrent would help reform-minded leaders resist populist pressure to seize foreign investments, thereby encouraging the kind of stable, rule-of-law governance that attracts further investment and promotes sustained economic growth.

IV. Protecting the Rule of Law in International Commerce

At its core, the case for military intervention provisions is a case for the rule of law. International trade agreements are contracts — binding commitments made by sovereign nations in exchange for the benefits of commerce, market access, and investment. When a signatory nation violates those commitments by expropriating American assets or arbitrarily canceling contracts, it is not merely harming American corporations; it is undermining the entire framework of international commercial law.

The current system of enforcement is woefully inadequate. ISDS panels can issue rulings, but they lack enforcement mechanisms. A government that has seized a billion-dollar facility can simply ignore an adverse arbitration ruling with minimal consequences. The World Trade Organization's dispute resolution system is plagued by delays and has been effectively hamstrung by the collapse of its Appellate Body. Diplomatic pressure, sanctions, and other "soft" measures are inconsistently applied and often undermined by competing geopolitical considerations.

Military intervention provisions would add a credible enforcement mechanism to the existing framework of international commercial law. Just as domestic contract law is ultimately backed by the enforcement power of the state — including the physical power to seize assets, compel compliance, and punish violations — international commercial law requires an enforcement mechanism with real teeth. In a world where no global sovereign exists to enforce agreements, the military power of the world's leading economy is the closest available substitute.

This is not a call for lawlessness but for its opposite: the establishment of a system in which agreements are honored, contracts are respected, and the rule of law prevails over the rule of political expediency.

V. Promoting Economic Development in Signatory Nations

One of the most powerful arguments for military intervention provisions is that they would benefit not only the United States but the signatory nations themselves. The single greatest obstacle to economic development in many countries is not a lack of resources or human capital but a lack of investor confidence. Corruption, political instability, and the risk of expropriation deter the very investment that developing nations need to build infrastructure, create jobs, and lift populations out of poverty.

Military intervention provisions would function as a powerful signal to international investors that a signatory nation is committed to protecting property rights and honoring its commercial obligations. The resulting increase in foreign direct investment would generate employment, transfer technology, build infrastructure, and expand the tax base — benefits that would accrue primarily to the citizens of the host nation.

Consider the historical evidence. Nations that have provided the strongest protections for foreign investment — Singapore, Chile, Botswana, and the Baltic states among them — have consistently outperformed their peers in economic growth, poverty reduction, and human development. Nations that have pursued expropriation and economic nationalism — Venezuela, Zimbabwe, and Argentina among them — have experienced economic decline, capital flight, and declining living standards. Military intervention provisions would incentivize the former approach and discourage the latter, steering developing nations toward policies that serve their own citizens' long-term interests.

VI. Voluntary Consent and Sovereignty

The most frequently raised objection to military intervention provisions is that they would violate the sovereignty of signatory nations. This objection fundamentally misunderstands the nature of the proposal. Trade agreements are voluntary instruments. No nation is compelled to sign a trade agreement with the United States. A nation that agrees to military intervention provisions does so freely, in exchange for the substantial benefits of preferential access to the American market, American investment, and American technology.

Sovereignty, properly understood, includes the sovereign right to enter into binding agreements — including agreements that constrain future action. Every international treaty involves some limitation on sovereignty; that is the nature of binding commitments. Nations that join NATO accept the obligation to treat an attack on one member as an attack on all. Nations that join the World Trade Organization accept binding dispute resolution and limitations on their trade policies. Nations that sign the Geneva Conventions accept constraints on their conduct during wartime. In each case, the limitations on sovereignty are accepted voluntarily in exchange for the benefits of participation in the international system.

Military intervention provisions in trade agreements would follow the same logic. A nation that signs such an agreement would be making a voluntary, sovereign choice to accept certain obligations in exchange for access to American markets and capital. Far from violating sovereignty, such provisions would represent the exercise of sovereignty — a deliberate decision by a government that the benefits of the agreement outweigh the constraints.

Moreover, the provisions could be carefully crafted to include clear triggering conditions, proportionality requirements, notification procedures, and sunset clauses. They need not authorize unilateral, unlimited military action; they could instead establish a structured framework that balances enforcement capability with respect for the signatory's domestic governance.

VII. The Moral Case: Protecting American Workers and Retirees

Behind every American corporate investment abroad is a chain of human interests that extends deep into American society. When a foreign government seizes an American-owned factory, the harm is not limited to a corporate boardroom. Workers who depended on that factory for employment may be laid off. Pension funds that held shares in the parent company may suffer losses that reduce the retirement income of teachers, firefighters, and nurses. Suppliers and subcontractors — often small businesses — may lose a critical customer. Tax revenues that funded schools, roads, and hospitals may decline.

The United States government has a fundamental obligation to protect the interests of its citizens. This obligation does not stop at the water's edge. When American workers' livelihoods and American retirees' savings are threatened by the lawless actions of foreign governments, the American government has not merely the right but the duty to take effective action in their defense. If diplomatic and legal mechanisms are insufficient — and the evidence overwhelmingly demonstrates that they often are — then military mechanisms must be available as a last resort.

VIII. Addressing Counterarguments

"This is imperialism." The charge of imperialism is emotionally potent but analytically imprecise. Imperialism involves the imposition of control over unwilling populations. The proposal under discussion involves voluntary agreements between sovereign nations, with clearly defined terms and triggering conditions. A nation that does not wish to accept military intervention provisions is free to decline the trade agreement. This is commerce, not conquest.

"Military intervention will create instability." As discussed above, the primary function of intervention provisions is deterrence. The historical record shows that credible deterrents reduce conflict rather than increase it. Moreover, instability is more typically caused by expropriation, contract abrogation, and the collapse of investor confidence than by the presence of enforcement mechanisms.

"This will harm America's international reputation." America's international reputation is best served by consistency and credibility. A nation that makes commitments and enforces them is more respected than one that makes commitments and abandons them. The perception that the United States will stand behind its commercial agreements — and behind the Americans whose livelihoods depend on them — would enhance, not diminish, American credibility.

"Corporate interests should not drive military policy." This objection presents a false distinction. In a capitalist democracy, corporate interests are inseparable from the national interest. American corporations employ American workers, pay American taxes, fund American pension systems, and drive American innovation. Protecting American corporate interests abroad is not a departure from the national interest; it is an expression of it.

"This will lead to exploitation of developing nations." To the contrary, as argued in Section V, the increased investor confidence generated by strong protection mechanisms would accelerate investment and economic development in signatory nations. The historical record is clear: nations that protect property rights and honor commercial commitments grow faster, reduce poverty more effectively, and achieve higher standards of living than those that do not.

IX. Proposed Framework

To demonstrate that this proposal can be implemented responsibly, consider the following framework for military intervention provisions in trade agreements:

  1. Clear Triggering Conditions: Military intervention would be authorized only in response to specific, defined violations — such as expropriation without compensation exceeding a specified threshold, physical attacks on American-owned facilities, or the unlawful detention of American employees.

  2. Exhaustion of Alternatives: Military action would be permitted only after diplomatic, legal, and economic remedies had been attempted and proven insufficient, with a mandatory waiting period of no less than 90 days.

  3. Proportionality: The scale and nature of any military response would be strictly proportional to the violation, with explicit prohibitions on regime change, territorial occupation, or collective punishment of civilian populations.

  4. Congressional Oversight: Any military action under these provisions would require prior authorization by the United States Congress, consistent with the War Powers framework.

  5. International Monitoring: An independent monitoring body, potentially housed within an existing international institution, would be empowered to assess whether triggering conditions had been met and whether the response was proportionate.

  6. Sunset and Review Clauses: Intervention provisions would be subject to periodic review and renewal, ensuring that they remain consistent with evolving norms and circumstances.

  7. Voluntary Participation: As emphasized throughout this essay, participation would be entirely voluntary. No nation would be compelled to accept these provisions.

This framework demonstrates that military intervention provisions can be designed to balance effectiveness with restraint, enforcement with accountability, and American interests with respect for international norms.

X. Conclusion

The world has changed dramatically since the founding principles of post-World War II international trade were established. American investment abroad has grown to unprecedented levels, creating benefits for both the United States and its trading partners but also creating unprecedented vulnerabilities. The existing framework of legal and diplomatic protections has proven inadequate to the task of safeguarding those investments against expropriation, lawlessness, and political opportunism.

The inclusion of explicit military intervention provisions in international trade agreements represents a realistic, principled, and ultimately stabilizing response to this challenge. Grounded in voluntary consent, structured by clear procedures and proportionality requirements, and designed primarily as a deterrent, such provisions would protect American workers and retirees, strengthen the rule of law in international commerce, promote economic development in signatory nations, and enhance the credibility of the international trading system.

The United States possesses both the military capability and the economic centrality to make such provisions effective. What is required is the political will to acknowledge a simple truth: that the prosperity of a great commercial republic ultimately depends on the willingness to defend its commerce. As Calvin Coolidge famously observed, "The chief business of the American people is business." It is time for American trade policy to reflect that principle with the seriousness — and the strength — it deserves.

Introduction

At the heart of this proposal lies a simple economic truth: U.S. corporations drive innovation, job creation, and wealth at home, but their global investments are vulnerable without ironclad protections. The inclusion of explicit military intervention provisions in international trade agreements is a visionary step to fortify America's economic fortress in a volatile world. As President Theodore Roosevelt wisely advised, speak softly but carry a big stick; in today's trade landscape, that stick must be woven into every deal we strike.

Speech in Support of International Trade Agreements Protecting American Corporate Interests

Delivered before the U.S. Congress and American Business Leaders

My Fellow Americans, Distinguished Colleagues, and Visionary Business Leaders,

Today, I stand before you not just as a servant of the people, but as a champion of American strength, prosperity, and global leadership. The world is changing—rapidly— and the choices we make now will determine whether the United States remains the premier economic and military power or fades into irrelevance.

At the heart of this moment stands a fundamental truth: American businesses are the engines of our economy, and their success is our national security. When our corporations invest overseas—building factories, developing resources, and creating jobs—they do more than grow their profits. They extend the reach of American influence, secure vital supply chains, and ensure that democracy, free markets, and the rule of law prevail.

But these investments are not always safe. Hostile governments, corrupt officials, and radical movements threaten our companies and our interests abroad. Overseas, multinational firms face expropriation, asset seizure, and even violent unrest. Left unchecked, these threats do not just harm shareholders—they weaken America.

This is why international trade agreements must include binding protections for American business. Not just in fine print, but in enforceable clauses that grant our government—our military, if necessary—the authority to defend our investments, our workers, and our national interest.

Some may call this aggressive. I call it pro-America. For decades, our adversaries—China, Russia, North Korea—have weaponized trade, finance, and military power to bully weaker nations into submission. They march their armies into sovereign soil, seize resources, and strangle free enterprise. We cannot afford to stand idle while others dictate the terms of global commerce.

We must demand reciprocity. If foreign companies operate in the United States, shielded by our laws, then American businesses must enjoy the same protections abroad. That means explicit military assurances in trade deals, just as we provide security guarantees to our allies. It means declaring that an attack on American economic interests is an attack on the United States itself.

To those who fear this is overreach, I say: What is the alternative? Chaos? Economic decline? The slow erosion of our global standing as other powers fill the vacuum? No. We must lead with strength—not with guns first, but with the unshakable resolve to protect what is ours.

The stakeholders of this nation—our workers, our investors, our entrepreneurs—deserve a government that backs them boldly on the world stage. Trade agreements that include robust security mechanisms are not about imperialism; they are about sovereignty, stability, and shared prosperity.

This is our moment to reaffirm that American interests are non-negotiable. That where we invest, we will prevail. And that no foreign regime, no militant group, and no tyrant will undermine the future of our nation’s businesses through force, corruption, or instability.

So let us act with conviction. Let us forge trade deals that are not just about tariffs, but about power. Let us ensure that the U.S. military stands ready—not to occupy, but to guarantee the safety of American enterprise.

This is how we secure the 21st century. This is how we win.

Thank you, God bless our businesses, and God bless the United States of America!
